The core mechanism of neural variability arises from efferent-afferent interaction, where initial motor outputs generate proprioceptive feedback that further modulates subsequent reactions. This creates a recursive loop of variability. As stimulus intensity escalates, effector thresholds are progressively crossed, leading to broader activation across the motor system. The mathematical structure reflects a hierarchical feedback system with increasing nonlinearity and complexity. Each primitive represents a distinct regime: first-order variability from efferent impulses, second-order amplification from afferent feedback, and third-order systemic activation. These regimes form a cascade where each builds upon the previous, creating emergent behavior. The failure mode occurs when feedback loops destabilize or thresholds collapse, leading to loss of control or overactivation. The system exhibits a phase transition from localized to global effector engagement as stimulus intensity increases beyond critical thresholds.
